newsitem.title: USA: Scientology-Germany war of words before rights report.
newsitem.headline: Scientology-Germany war of words before rights report.

text.p: On the eve of a State Department report expected to criticise Germany for its treatment of Scientologists, the war of words heated up on Wednesday between Bonn and the Los Angeles-based church.

The Church of Scientology accused German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's conservative party in Bavaria of "Teutonic arrogance and insensitivity" towards criticism that church members were discriminated against.
Meanwhile, Bavaria, which has banned Scientologists from holding public office, called on the German government to take a tougher stance against the group.
And the head of a German parliamentary committee investigating what it calls "so-called sects" said Bonn had acted correctly in keeping a close eye on Scientology.
Rev. Heber Jentzsch, President of the Church of Scientology International, accused the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) -- sister party of Kohl's Christian Democrats -- of "strong-arm rhetoric."

He said the party's suggestion that the State Department had "fallen for" the Scientologists "harkens back to Nazi accusations that then President Roosevelt was surrounded by Jewish advisers who whispered tales of persecution in his ears."

"CSU politicians think their egos are more important than the right of German citizens to provide for their families, send their children to school and live their lives free of government harassment and intimidation," said Jentzsch.
"While (CSU leader Bernd) Protzner and (Bavarian) Interior Minister Guenther Beckstein wallow in rhetoric, basic human rights are being denied our parishoners in Germany," he said.
The statement came a day before the State Department was issuing its annual report on human rights around the world.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns and other U.S. officials said the situation of Scientologists in Germany would be addressed in the report be published on Thursday.
Four previous editions of the report have raised U.S. concerns over Bonn's attitude to Scientology, which Germany regards as a potential threat to the public.
On Monday, Burns told reporters Scientologists are the target of discrimination in Germany and prompted "some unfortunate reactions" by members of the German government.

But he said Scientologists and Hollywood supporters had made "outrageous" comparisons of the Bonn government to Germany's former Nazi rulers. Movie stars John Travolta and Tom Cruise are Scientologists, as is jazz pianist Chick Corea.

Bavaria's Interior Minister Beckstein told German radio on Wednesday his state and another had introduced a resolution in the upper house of parliament "to achieve co-ordinated and concerted action in all German states against Scientology."
And Ronald Pofall, head of a parliamentary committee investigating the issue, said: "Some of the things that Scientology does in Germany are legally problematic."
"We should also make it clear to the U.S. that Scientologists are trying to do things here that they are not allowed to under the cover of a religion," said Pofall.
Scientology is a religious philosophy founded in 1954 by science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard. Germany regards it not as a religion but an economic organisation exploiting its members.
